walkthrough:
Sort Out The Two Y-Axes**
You are sitting with two different bar series. Grey bars are mean daily air temperature on the left axis in $^{\circ}\text{C}$. White bars are mean monthly milk yield per cow on the right axis in $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$. Focus only on April, May, June, July, August.

Describe Opposite Trends With Numbers**
Grey bars get taller from April to August, so temperature rises. White bars get shorter, so milk yield falls. To earn both marks you must quote figures: about $10 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ rising to about $18 ^{\circ}\text{C}$, while yield falls from about 792-798 to about 711-716 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$.

Final answer: From April to August temperature increases and milk yield decreases. April $10 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and approx. 795 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$, August $18 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and approx. 713 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$.

Recall what Fig. 4.2 proved about temperature and yield, and what that tells you about nature versus nurture.
Use the clue that 20 different genes affect body temperature and that heat-tolerant breeds differ genetically from Holsteins to decide if one gene or many genes are involved.
walkthrough:
Recognise Continuous Variation**
Milk yield is measured in $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$ and can take any value between extremes, for example 690 to 800. There are no sharp categories, only intermediates. That is the hallmark of continuous variation, not discontinuous variation which has distinct phenotypes like blood groups.

Link Environment To The Graph**
Fig. 4.2 shows yield changes as air temperature changes, so temperature is an environmental factor causing phenotypic variation. Same genotype can give different yield in different temperatures.

Link Genes To Breed Differences**
Twenty genes have alleles found only in heat-tolerant cattle, and heat-tolerant cattle yield less than Holsteins when no heat stress occurs. That shows many genes each have a small additive effect. This is polygenic inheritance, a genetic cause of continuous variation.

Final answer: Continuous variation as milk yield shows a range with intermediates and no distinct classes. Caused by environment - air temperature affects yield; and by genetics - polygenic, many genes affect yield.

walkthrough:
See The Overall Benefit**
In both months the grey bar for Holstein with SLICK is higher than the white bar for normal Holstein. So the dominant SLICK allele increases yield in both cool and warm conditions.

Spot That The Benefit Is Bigger When Warm**
In March at $5 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ there is little heat stress, so the gap is small, about 15 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$. In September at $14 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ normal Holsteins drop to about 695 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$ while SLICK cattle stay near 775 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$. The gap is much larger.

Explain Maintenance Of Yield**
Short hair from reduced hair growth helps lose heat, so SLICK cattle resist heat stress and maintain milk yield when temperature rises, while normal cattle show a large fall. Always quote paired data with units to prove the pattern.

Final answer: SLICK allele increases milk yield at both temperatures. Small difference in March at $5 ^{\circ}\text{C}$; larger difference in September at $14 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ as SLICK cattle maintain yield. e.g. March 780-785 vs 795-800, September 690-700 vs 770-780 $\text{kg cow}^{-1}$.

walkthrough:
State The Similarities First**
Both methods aim to put the dominant SLICK allele into Holsteins so first offspring carry it. Both are artificial selection by humans, not natural selection. Presence can be confirmed by DNA testing or seeing short hair.

Contrast Speed And Scale**
Gene editing replicates the single nucleotide deletion directly in the zygote, so effect is immediate in one generation. Selective breeding needs crossing Senepol with Holstein then repeated back-crossing over many generations to recover Holstein type while keeping SLICK.

Contrast Precision And Variation**
Editing changes only the PRLR gene, so the high-yield Holstein genome and heterozygosity are maintained. Breeding mixes whole genomes, so many genes are affected, variation is lost, undesirable Senepol traits are introduced and outbreeding is needed. That is why editing needs lab methods and regulatory approval, while breeding uses physiological mating on the farm with no such approval.

Build Paired Comparisons**
For full marks write in pairs: all offspring get allele by editing vs only some by breeding; lab embryo work vs farm mating; retains desirable characteristics vs risks losing them. Also note both can have negative or unknown effects that need checking.

Final answer: Similarities: both give offspring with SLICK allele; both artificial by humans. Differences: gene editing immediate in one generation vs selective breeding over many generations; editing affects only PRLR gene vs breeding mixes many genes; editing on embryos/cells in lab vs breeding by mating/AI on farm; editing maintains heterozygosity/variation and high yield traits vs breeding causes loss and needs outbreeding; editing needs regulatory approval and testing for off-target effects.
